summary: Defines the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol. It uses an election among routers on a LAN to decide which one takes responsibility for a shared virtual router, so hosts keep a working default gateway if one router fails. It was replaced by RFC 3768.

eli5.summary: Two crossing guards share one job. If the main guard goes home sick, the other steps in so children can still cross.

questions: how does virtual router redundancy work
subtitle: Automatic failover when routers share a virtual IP address.

tldr.problem: When hosts use a single default router IP address, they lose connectivity if that router fails, even if other routers are available on the network.
tldr.mechanism: VRRP runs an election among multiple routers on a LAN to decide which one actively owns and forwards traffic for a shared virtual IP address. If the active router fails, a backup takes over automatically.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can use a virtual IP as their default gateway without needing to know about failover. The protocol was replaced by RFC 3768.

today: RFC 2338 is a Proposed Standard from April 1998 and was obsoleted by RFC 3768, which is the current standard for VRRP.

sections.title: The Problem of the Single Router
sections.content:
End hosts on a network need to know how to reach the rest of the Internet. The simplest way is to configure them with a default router: an IP address to send all outgoing traffic to. However, if that router fails, all those hosts lose connectivity, even if other routers on the same network segment could serve the same purpose. This is a single point of failure.

Dynamic routing protocols like OSPF can solve this, but they require running on every end host, which is impractical due to configuration complexity and processing overhead. VRRP offers a lighter-weight alternative: it lets multiple routers cooperate to maintain a single, virtual router IP address that can fail over automatically.
sections.eli5: If you only know one way to get out of your neighborhood, and that path breaks, you are stuck. VRRP is like having two guards so the route always works.

sections.title: How VRRP Works
sections.content:
VRRP runs on multiple routers on a local area network (LAN) to elect one as the Master for a virtual router. Each virtual router is identified by a Virtual Router Identifier (VRID) and owns one or more IP addresses. The Master router forwards packets destined for those virtual addresses and answers ARP requests for them, making it transparent to end hosts which physical router is active.

All VRRP traffic between routers uses IP multicast to the address 224.0.0.18. The Master periodically sends Advertisement messages to announce its presence. Backup routers listen passively. If the Master stops sending advertisements, the highest-priority Backup waits a brief timeout and takes over as Master. The IP address owner (the router that owns the virtual IP as a real interface address) always becomes Master when it is available, ensuring the most preferred router is in control.
sections.eli5: The routers talk to each other over the network to agree on who is in charge. If the boss router stops talking, the deputy takes over within a second or so.

sections.title: The VRRP Packet and Priority
sections.content:
VRRP packets are IP packets with protocol number 112. Each packet contains a priority field that controls who becomes Master. The router that owns the virtual IP address must use priority 255 (the highest). Backup routers use priorities between 1 and 254, with a default of 100. The priority zero has special meaning: if the Master sends an advertisement with priority zero, it is announcing that it is leaving office, triggering backups to elect a new Master immediately without waiting for a timeout.

The packet also includes the Virtual Router ID, the list of IP addresses the virtual router owns, an advertisement interval (default 1 second), and an authentication method (no authentication, simple text password, or IP Authentication Header). The authentication is unique per interface, allowing the same VRID to be used with different configurations on different LANs.
sections.eli5: The message routers send to each other says "I am in charge and my strength is 100" (or 255 for the owner). If priority is 0, it means "I am giving up."

sections.title: Master Election and State Transitions
sections.content:
VRRP defines three states. When a router starts up, it enters Initialize. If its priority is 255 (it is the address owner), it immediately becomes Master, sends an announcement, and starts forwarding. Otherwise, it becomes Backup and listens for advertisements from the Master.

In the Backup state, a router must not answer ARP requests for the virtual address or accept packets sent to it. It monitors the Master's advertisements. If the master timeout expires without hearing from the Master, the Backup transitions to Master. If a higher-priority backup is present and its advertisements are heard, the current Master yields to it only if that backup's priority is strictly higher, or if preemption is enabled and the priorities are equal. This prevents unnecessary churn when multiple routers have equal priority.
sections.eli5: Backup routers sit quietly waiting. When the Master stops talking (times out), the one with the highest strength becomes the new Master. If two guards have equal strength, they stick with whoever was Master rather than constantly switching.

sections.title: The Virtual MAC Address
sections.content:
Each virtual router is assigned a well-known IEEE 802 MAC address of the form 00-00-5E-00-01-{VRID}, where {VRID} is the Virtual Router Identifier. This allows bridges to learn the location of the virtual router on the network. When the Master forwards traffic, it uses the virtual MAC as the source address in packets it sends, so bridges learn the virtual router's location and do not flood traffic destined for the virtual address.

When a Master transitions to Backup, it stops using the virtual MAC, preventing the bridge from learning the wrong location. The new Master will use the virtual MAC in its outbound packets. FDDI and Token Ring networks have special requirements for handling virtual MAC addresses, but the principle remains the same: use the known virtual MAC to keep bridge learning tables correct.
sections.eli5: The virtual router has its own fake address label on the network. Whichever guard is in charge uses that label when sending things out, so the network knows where to send replies.
